The club of Heracles. They derive it etymologically from ῥοπή (force) and ἀλοιᾶν (to thresh). And δαπέδοιο from the root.

17 scholion on line 141

With their own wedges: he means the parts around the mast-holder that surround and strengthen the mast. Throughout, the comparison is sound and vigorous. For he likens the fir tree to a mast because of its straightness and tall growth; for that tree also stands like a mast. And he likens the sudden appearance of the hero to a wintry season, and his strength to a violent wind. The phrase "with their own wedges" refers to the earth that surrounds the root of the fir tree; for those mounds of earth also surrounded it like wedges, and the †τόνοι† held the place of forestays, stretched tight.

22 Πέρινθος Wilamowitz : Περιθόας Τρίγξ Merkel, comparing Strabo XVII 825 : Φρίξ. Wilamowitz in the same place wishes to retain the traditional reading. He proposes Λυκίας instead of Λιβύης, ad loc.

In the work To Eidotheos (fr. 9 M. IV 498) he says that Hylas became the beloved of Polyphemus and not of Heracles. But Onasus in the first book of his Amazonica (41 fr. 1 a J.) sets out the story more truthfully: he was not snatched by nymphs, but fell into a spring and so died.
It is unseemly for a young man to carry a water-jar; Homer (Od. 7.20) appropriately has a maiden do so. It would have been more plausible to say an amphora, as Callimachus does (fr. 546 Schn.).
